content: 1. The National Tuberculosis Program (NTP) employs specific diagnostic algorithms for detecting drug-resistant tuberculosis (DR-TB). These algorithms include rapid diagnostic tests such as the Xpert MTB/RIF assay, line probe assays (LPA), and other rapid tests. Additionally, conventional methods like solid and liquid culture drug susceptibility testing (DST) are utilized. The criteria for testing DR-TB include the use of rapid diagnostics or conventional DST, depending on the clinical scenario. 2. Laboratories involved in DR-TB management provide various services, including rapid diagnostic tests, solid and liquid culture methods, and DST for first-line drugs (FLDs) and second-line drugs (SLDs). The availability and quality assurance (QA) of these services are critical for accurate diagnosis and treatment. 3. The National TB Reference Laboratory (NTRL) operates either in the public or private sector, with administrative control depending on its affiliation. The NTRL may also collaborate with supranational laboratories for quality assurance and advanced testing. The culture methods used at the NTRL include solid and liquid cultures, with specific turnaround times for results. DST methods are employed to test FLDs and SLDs, with external QA conducted for certain drugs. 4. The availability and use of SLDs vary across different health sectors, including the NTP, non-NTP public sector, and private sector. Drugs such as streptomycin, kanamycin, amikacin, capreomycin, fluoroquinolones (e.g., levofloxacin, moxifloxacin), and newer agents like bedaquiline and delamanid are included in treatment regimens. Policies regarding the purchase of SLDs, including prescription requirements, differ between sectors. 5. Major DR-TB care providers are evaluated for their drug management capacities, including ordering, procurement, quality assurance, storage, distribution, and data management systems. Any stock-outs of SLDs in the past five years are analyzed to identify reasons and lessons learned. 6. National treatment guidelines for multidrug-resistant TB (MDR-TB) are in use, and policies on hospitalization for MDR-TB patients are outlined. Laboratory-confirmed rifampicin-resistant TB (RR-TB) or MDR-TB patients are linked to treatment sites for initiation and continuation of therapy. Treatment regimens are decided based on standardized or individualized approaches, with empirical treatment used in specific cases. 7. Treatment adherence is ensured through various measures, including the provision of free SLDs, free diagnosis, and patient support systems. Adverse drug reactions (ADRs) to SLDs are managed with available drugs, and care providers are trained in their use. ADRs are reported to the national pharmacovigilance center and recorded in the TB register. 8. Infection control measures are implemented in health facilities managing DR-TB patients. These include protocols for hospitalized patients, such as isolation and ventilation systems, to prevent the spread of infection. Treatment outcomes are evaluated, recorded, and reported following WHO guidelines, with electronic recording and reporting systems applied. 9. Public-private mix (PPM) models for DR-TB care involve collaboration between the NTP and private entities. Training and capacity-building activities are conducted for PPM providers, with plans for enhancing the capacity of both NTP and non-NTP staff. The readiness of the NTP to expand DR-TB care through PPM is assessed. 10. Existing links between the NTP and non-NTP providers for DR-TB care are described, including strengths, weaknesses, opportunities, and threats (SWOT) of these collaborations. Providers with the potential to become PPM partners are identified, and their readiness to manage DR-TB is evaluated. 11. Comprehensive care for DR-TB patients involves addressing clinical, managerial, financial, and emotional challenges. Public-private and public-public collaborations extend beyond clinical care to include a wide range of partners to ensure holistic support for patients. 12. The supply and management procedures for SLDs are described, including procurement, storage, and distribution. Infection control measures in facilities managing DR-TB patients are detailed, and patient satisfaction with treatment is assessed through interviews. 13. The financial implications of DR-TB management in the private sector are analyzed, including costs borne by patients, the national program, and private providers. This includes expenses related to diagnosis, treatment, and social support. 14. Plans for scaling up programmatic management of drug-resistant TB (PMDT) and PPM DR-TB are outlined, with specific steps to enhance capacity, ensure drug supply, and improve supervision and monitoring of trained providers. 15. A checklist is provided to assess the preparedness of non-NTP TB care providers for PPM DR-TB, covering aspects such as TB services offered, treatment supervision, drug supply, reporting, and experience in public health and TB control.
